geology-impact-craters: Impact craters are the scars of cosmic collisions — circular depressions blasted when asteroids or comets strike the surface. The energy of impact vaporizes rock, excavates a bowl, and throws debris for hundreds of kilometres. Earth has over 200 confirmed craters, but that is a small fraction of the original count: erosion, plate tectonics, and vegetation erase most. Craters like Meteor Crater in Arizona preserve a snapshot of a moment of violence.
geology-meteorites: Meteorites are rocks from space that survive the fiery plunge through the atmosphere and land on Earth. Most are fragments of asteroids, some come from the Moon and Mars, and a rare few may be from other planets' moons. Each one carries a record of the early solar system, older than any rock on Earth. Collectors and scientists prize them — a fresh fall can arrive with a boom and a trail of scorched sky.
geology-meteorite-types: Meteorites fall into three families: stony meteorites, the most common, made of silicate minerals; iron meteorites, dense metallic masses from shattered asteroid cores; and stony-irons, rare mixtures of both. Stony meteorites include chondrites, which hold tiny glassy spheres — chondrules — dating from the solar system's birth. Iron meteorites show Widmanstätten patterns, crystalline structures that form only over millions of years of slow cooling inside asteroids.
geology-meteorite-impacts: A meteorite impact releases energy equal to mass times velocity squared — so a small rock hits like a bomb. The Chicxulub impact 66 million years ago released more energy than a billion atomic bombs and ended the dinosaurs. Even metre-sized rocks punch through the atmosphere and scatter debris over towns. A 10-kilometre object — rare but inevitable over geological time — can reshape global climate.
geology-crater-formation: A crater forms in three acts: compression, when the impactor's energy vaporizes rock and drives a shock wave through the ground; excavation, when the shock blasts a bowl out at high speed; and modification, when the steep walls slump and the crater settles. Small craters stay simple bowls; large ones develop central peaks and ringed terraces as the shocked rock rebounds. The whole drama takes seconds — a geological event over in a blink.
geology-chicxulub-crater: The Chicxulub crater, buried under Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, is the most famous impact scar on Earth: a 180-kilometre-wide structure from the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs 66 million years ago. The impact threw up a dust veil that darkened the sky for months, freezing the climate. Geologists found it through its ring of buried rock and worldwide layer of iridium, an element rare on Earth but common in asteroids.
geology-meteor-craters: Meteor Crater in Arizona is the best-preserved impact crater on Earth — a 1.2-kilometre bowl blasted about 50,000 years ago by an iron meteorite. The desert climate kept its rim sharp, and visitors can see upturned rock layers pushed out from the blast. Long thought volcanic, it took mining engineer Daniel Barringer, who drilled for the buried meteorite, to prove the impact origin. The meteorite mostly vaporized on impact.
geology-tektites: Tektites are small, glassy blobs — often black, green, or brown — flung thousands of kilometres from large impacts. Molten rock splashed high into the atmosphere cools into droplets and aerodynamically sculpted shapes before falling back to Earth. They form strewn fields, like the Australasian tektites spread across a third of the planet from a single impact. Tektites are nature's impact souvenirs, and their composition matches the target rock, not the meteorite.
geology-impact-breccia: Impact breccia is the rubble of a crater: angular rock fragments, shocked and shattered by the blast, cemented together in a matrix of pulverized debris. It fills the crater floor, lines the walls, and forms thick deposits around the rim. Breccia layers are the signature of impact — geologists identify ancient craters by finding this distinctive jumble of broken rock. Some breccias contain glass formed by impact melting, recording the violence of the strike.
geology-shocked-quartz: Shocked quartz is quartz whose crystal structure has been deformed by the intense pressure of an impact — typically over 10 gigapascals. Under the microscope it shows parallel lines called planar deformation features, invisible to the naked eye but unmistakable to a geologist. Shock features like these are diagnostic proof of impact, since no ordinary volcanic or tectonic process can produce them. Shocked quartz found in a worldwide clay layer helped confirm the Chicxulub impact.
geology-impact-spherules: Impact spherules are tiny, often glassy or crystalline beads formed when impact melt sprays into the air and solidifies into droplets. They fall back to Earth and form a thin, distinctive layer that can be traced across continents — like the tektite-strewn layer from Chicxulub found from Texas to Haiti. Spherule layers are time markers: find one, and you have dated the same catastrophe on two continents. They help geologists count Earth's largest impact events.
geology-tsunami-impacts: An ocean impact can generate tsunami waves dwarfing any earthquake-driven one. When a large object slams into the sea, it displaces a wall of water that races outward at hundreds of kilometres per hour. The Chicxulub impact's tsunami may have been hundreds of metres high when it hit distant coastlines. Evidence survives as thick, chaotic sediment beds — 'impact tsunamites' — deposited far inland. Geologists map these layers to reconstruct ancient ocean impacts.
geology-impact-extinction: Impacts can end eras. The Chicxulub impact 66 million years ago wiped out three-quarters of species, ending the dinosaurs and opening the door for mammals. Other impact layers correlate with smaller extinction events, though most mass extinctions have volcanic or climatic causes. The danger is probabilistic: large impacts are rare, but their effects are global and sudden. Studying past impact extinctions tells us what another major strike could do to our civilization.
geology-bolide: A bolide is a spectacular meteor — a fireball bright enough to light up the night sky, often with explosions and sonic booms. Strictly, the term refers to an impactor that explodes in the atmosphere, as the Chelyabinsk meteor did in 2013, shattering windows across Russian cities. Bolides come from asteroids and comets whose orbits cross Earth's. Tracking networks now record them nightly, mapping the small objects that constantly brush our planet.
geology-meteorite-hunting: Meteorite hunting combines science and treasure hunting: freshly fallen meteorites are valuable to collectors and researchers alike. The best hunting grounds are deserts and ice sheets, where dark meteorites stand out against light surfaces and dry or cold conditions preserve them. Antarctic meteorites concentrate where ice flow pushes them against mountain ranges — thousands are collected each season. Finders often scan with metal detectors, since many meteorites are rich in iron.
geology-meteorite-antarctica: Antarctica is the world's meteorite treasure chest: over 60,000 specimens collected so far, many from asteroids, the Moon, and Mars. The ice does two jobs — it preserves meteorites for tens of thousands of years, and its slow flow concentrates them along mountain barriers where they surface again. A dark rock on white ice is easy to spot, making search efficient. Martian meteorites from Antarctica helped prove that Mars once had water.
geology-chelyabinsk: The Chelyabinsk meteor exploded over Russia in February 2013 with the force of roughly 30 Hiroshima bombs. The 20-metre asteroid entered at hypersonic speed and burst about 30 kilometres up, its flash outshining the sun and its shockwave blowing out windows across the city, injuring over a thousand people. Thousands of fragments, some weighing hundreds of kilograms, fell into a frozen lake. It was the largest airburst since the 1908 Tunguska event.
geology-tunguska: The Tunguska event of 1908 flattened over 2,000 square kilometres of Siberian forest with no crater left behind — the asteroid or comet exploded several kilometres above the ground in an airburst. Eyewitnesses reported a blinding flash, a pillar of fire, and tremors felt hundreds of kilometres away. Trees lay felled in a radial pattern around ground zero, but almost no impactor material was ever found. It remains the largest cosmic impact in recorded history.
geology-asteroid-defense: Asteroid defense is the effort to find and deflect objects that could threaten Earth. Telescopes map near-Earth asteroids, cataloguing their orbits decades in advance; the goal is to spot a dangerous one with years of lead time. Deflection options include nudging the asteroid with a spacecraft impact, towing it with gravity, or — as a last resort — nuclear blasts. The 2022 DART mission proved the kinetic-impact method works by changing an asteroid's orbit.
geology-dart-mission: NASA's DART mission was the first planetary defense test: in September 2022, a spacecraft deliberately slammed into the asteroid Dimorphos at about 6 kilometres per second. The impact shortened the asteroid's orbit around its companion by 32 minutes — far more than expected, as the collision ejected tonnes of debris that added thrust. The test proved that a well-aimed spacecraft can change an asteroid's path, turning a sci-fi idea into an engineering capability.
geology-planetary-geology: Planetary geology applies Earth's rock science to other worlds — the Moon, Mars, Venus, and beyond. The same tools work everywhere: craters date surfaces, lava flows tell of volcanic pasts, and river channels reveal flowing water. Comparing planets teaches us about Earth, too — Venus shows what runaway greenhouse does, Mars shows a world that lost its water. Planetary geologists now walk alien landscapes through rovers, orbiters, and sample returns.
geology-mars-geology: Mars is a geologist's paradise: no oceans, weak erosion, and a thin atmosphere leave billions of years of history exposed. Its surface shows giant volcanoes, canyon systems, dried riverbeds, polar ice caps, and dust storms that reshape the landscape. Rover missions have found rocks formed in ancient lakes and rivers, proving Mars was once warm and wet. Its crust preserves the record of a planet that lost most of its atmosphere and water.
geology-olympus-mons: Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in the solar system — about 22 kilometres high, nearly three times Everest, and wide enough to cover France. It is a shield volcano built by countless thin lava flows, its gentle slopes forming over billions of years of steady eruption. Mars lacks plate tectonics, so the volcano stayed over its magma source and kept building. Its summit caldera is 80 kilometres across.
geology-valles-marineris: Valles Marineris is the solar system's grandest canyon: a system of chasms stretching 4,000 kilometres across Mars, up to 200 kilometres wide and 7 kilometres deep. It likely formed when the crust swelled over the Tharsis volcanic bulge and cracked, with landslides and water later widening the gorges. Its walls expose kilometres of Martian strata, a natural cross-section of the planet's history. Earth's Grand Canyon would fit comfortably inside one of its side canyons.
geology-mars-water-history: Mars was once a water world. Rovers and orbiters show ancient river deltas, lake beds, and minerals that form only in liquid water — Mars had lakes and rivers for its first billion years. Then its magnetic field faded and the atmosphere thinned, letting water escape to space or freeze into the ground. Today water survives as polar ice, subsurface ice, and briny streaks, driving Mars exploration.
geology-moon-geology: The Moon is a fossil of the early solar system, its surface barely changed for billions of years. It formed about 4.5 billion years ago, likely from debris of a giant impact with Earth, then melted and differentiated into crust, mantle, and core. Its light highlands are ancient anorthosite; the dark maria are younger basalt lava plains. Without plate tectonics or weather, the Moon's craters record the bombardment history of the inner solar system.
geology-lunar-maria: The lunar maria are the dark, smooth plains that form the 'man in the moon' — giant basins flooded with lava about 3 to 4 billion years ago. Early astronomers called them seas, but they are basalt flows erupted when huge impacts cracked the Moon's crust and magma welled up. The basalt is rich in iron and titanium, giving it a darker colour than the highlands, with craters dotting the lava plains.
geology-moon-regolith: Lunar regolith is the Moon's soil: a layer of shattered rock and glass up to several metres thick, ground up by billions of years of meteorite impacts. Without wind or water, particles stay sharp and angular, and tiny glass beads formed by impact melting are mixed in. Astronauts found it so fine and clingy it got into everything. It also holds trapped solar-wind gases and, scientists hope, water ice at the poles.
geology-venus-geology: Venus is Earth's toxic twin: similar in size and composition, but wrapped in a crushing carbon-dioxide atmosphere and 460°C surface heat. Radar mapping revealed a world of vast volcanic plains, thousands of volcanoes, and strange deformed terrain called tesserae. Venus shows almost no impact craters on much of its surface — evidence that huge volcanic resurfacing events wiped them out. Its runaway greenhouse offers a warning about Earth's climate direction.
geology-io-volcanoes: Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanically active world known — over 400 active volcanoes, powered not by internal heat but by tidal flexing as Jupiter's gravity kneads the moon. Sulphur and sulphur dioxide paint Io yellow, orange, and red, and eruptions can blast plumes hundreds of kilometres high. Its lava lakes and calderas resemble ancient Earth. Io's restless surface is geologically young, resurfaced so fast that almost no impact craters survive.
geology-europa-geology: Europa, one of Jupiter's large moons, hides an ocean beneath a cracked ice shell. Its surface is young and smooth, crisscrossed by brown ridges and bands where the ice shell has fractured and shifted — evidence of a mobile ice crust over liquid water. Tidal heating keeps the ocean liquid, making Europa a prime candidate for hosting life. Future missions will study its plumes for chemistry that might betray biology below.
geology-titan-geology: Titan, Saturn's largest moon, has geology eerily like Earth's — but made of exotic materials. Its thick orange atmosphere hides rivers, lakes, and seas of liquid methane and ethane, with rain, dunes, and river deltas carved by hydrocarbon weather. Its water-ice crust behaves like rock, and scientists suspect a liquid water ocean deep below. Titan is the only moon with a dense atmosphere, its geological cycle running on methane instead of water.
geology-mercury-geology: Mercury is a scorched, cratered world with a surprisingly iron-rich core that takes up most of its volume. Its surface shows ancient lava plains, giant impact basins like the Caloris basin, and strange 'hollows' — pits that may be carved by vaporized minerals. Mercury's day lasts two of its years, and surface temperatures swing hundreds of degrees. Despite the extremes, water ice hides in permanently shadowed polar craters, shielded from the Sun's heat.
geology-planetary-crusts: Every rocky world wears a crust, but they differ wildly: Earth's thin, recycled crust moves on plates; Mars's thick, static crust preserves ancient terrain; the Moon's crust is battered anorthosite; Venus's is young volcanic plains; Mercury's is cratered and iron-rich. Crustal thickness and behaviour depend on a planet's size, heat, and water. Comparing crusts reveals how the same building blocks produce such different worlds — and why Earth's active crust is so unusual.
geology-exoplanet-geology: Geology now extends beyond the solar system: telescopes measure the density, composition, and even weather of planets around other stars. Most exoplanets are thought to be rocky super-Earths or lava worlds, and some may have plate tectonics or oceans. Astronomers infer surfaces from spectra — molecules like water, carbon dioxide, and methane in their atmospheres. We cannot yet see exoplanet rocks directly, but the first geological observations of alien worlds are already underway.
geology-asteroid-geology: Asteroids are leftover building blocks of the solar system — small worlds with their own geology. Missions like Hayabusa2 and OSIRIS-REx have touched two of them, finding regolith, boulders, and organic molecules, and returning samples to Earth. Many asteroids are rubble piles: loose collections of rock held together by gravity, reshaped by impacts and even by sunlight. Their compositions range from primitive carbon-rich material to molten metal cores of shattered protoplanets.
geology-comet-geology: Comets are icy bodies from the solar system's deep freeze, preserving pristine material from its birth. A comet's 'dirty snowball' holds water ice, carbon dioxide, dust, and complex organics; near the Sun, ices vaporize and blast jets that form the glowing coma and tail. The Rosetta mission orbited comet 67P and found cliffs, pits, and plains shaped by sublimation. Comets may have delivered water and organics to early Earth.
geology-planetary-regolith: Regolith — loose surface debris — covers nearly every solid world. On the Moon it is pulverized impact breccia; on Mars it is dust and volcanic sand sculpted into dunes; on asteroids it is a loose gravel pile; on Earth it is our own soil and sediment. Regolith records a world's history: each impact layer and wind streak is a page. It is also the material future explorers will mine and build with.
geology-planetary-rovers: Rovers are robotic field geologists. NASA's Mars rovers carry cameras, spectrometers, drills, and even a miniature lab; they have found riverbeds, discovered the chemistry for life, and drilled ancient lake sediments. The Mars 2020 Perseverance rover collects rock cores for return to Earth, while China's Zhurong explored the red plains. Driving a rover is slow — every metre is planned from orbit — but together they have rewritten the story of Mars.
geology-astrogeology: Astrogeology is the study of geology beyond Earth — craters, volcanoes, ice, and oceans on other worlds. The US Geological Survey's astrogeology program, founded to support the Apollo missions, still maps the Moon, Mars, and beyond today. Astrogeologists compare planetary surfaces to Earth's geology to understand how worlds evolve, and they train astronauts in field geology. Every mission to another world carries a piece of Earth's geological method with it.
